content:
I have been a fan and customer of Sonos for many years, starting from the original Sonos One. So when I heard about two years ago that Sonos was moving into the over-ear headphone market, I knew I had to give them a try. The Sonos Ace looks great, is comfortable to wear, and brings several interesting features within the Sonos ecosystem. But as a pair of high-end headphones, there were still a few areas where I felt things could be better, such as stronger bass, better ANC (active noise cancellation), and a better app experience. However, the brand-new Sonos Ace Ultra seems to have systematically addressed almost every piece of feedback from me and most customers. I have used them for nearly a month as my primary headphones, relying on them whether travelling, editing videos, working out, walking around, or just listening to music day-to-day. So I have a thorough grasp of them, and here is what you need to know.

Be sure to also check out our Sonos Ace Ultra hands-on video review:

At first glance, the Sonos Ace Ultra and the original Sonos Ace do not look very different. Sonos has kept the same minimalist, understated design, with only slightly repositioned chrome accents and a few more colour options. But the biggest differences are actually inside the headphones.

Differences between the original Sonos Ace and Ace Ultra

Below are some of the biggest changes from the original Sonos Ace to the Ace Ultra:

  • Redesigned 40mm driver unit
  • An array of 10 microphones, two more than the previous generation
  • Improved adaptive ANC, claimed to double the noise cancellation performance, and able to automatically adjust based on changes in glasses, hair, and the seal of the ear cups
  • Longer battery life, up to 35 hours with ANC enabled
  • Bluetooth 6.0, up from 5.4 in the previous generation
  • Expanded EQ options, offering three presets and one advanced eight-band EQ
  • Headphones can connect to the Sonos ecosystem
  • User-replaceable battery
  • Updated materials for the ear cup and headband padding
  • Wider ear cup rotation, allowing them to lay flat and hang around the neck
  • Two new colours: Agave and Sand

Among these changes, what I noticed most was the redesigned acoustic architecture, the better bass response, and the stronger ANC. When using the original Sonos Ace, I would occasionally hear a faint hissing sound in ANC mode. Although it was rare, I did notice it. The Sonos Ace Ultra has essentially solved this issue. You still get to keep several excellent specs from the previous generation, such as:

  • Spatial audio and Dolby Atmos
  • Dynamic head tracking
  • Support for lossless audio playback on supported devices
  • USB-C and 3.5mm wired audio input
  • Bluetooth multipoint connection
  • Fast charging, with three minutes of charging providing up to three hours of playback
  • TV Audio Swap functionality when used with compatible Sonos soundbars

They retain the same high-quality design, combining plastic and metal to deliver a premium yet lightweight feel. The Sonos Ace Ultra also keeps the magnetic swappable ear cups, and one of the best points I have noticed is that the new EQ settings really let me fine-tune the sound to my personal preference. But as headphones for daily use, how do they actually perform?

User experience

At the end of the day, the numbers on the spec sheet are easy to write, but what impressed me most about the Ace Ultra is that it sounds noticeably better in real-world use. The biggest criticism of the original Sonos Ace was insufficient bass depth. The bass was actually not bad, but for a pair of US$450 headphones, I felt it left something to be desired. I listen to a lot of R&B, hip-hop, and pop music, so bass is very important to me. I wanted stronger low-frequency impact, to really feel the bass. The Ace Ultra finally delivers the experience I was looking for.

The low-frequency impact and depth have been substantially improved. But it is worth noting that Sonos has not simply turned up the bass. Any brand can crank up the bass, but the challenge is maintaining separation so the bass does not drown out the vocals, instruments, and highs. That is where the Ace Ultra truly surprised me. The bass is fuller, yet the vocals remain clear, sharp, and easy to hear. And it is not just for music; all media sounds great, whether it is podcasts, movies, or the YouTube videos I watch, with consistently excellent performance across all types of media playback.

The improvement in ANC is also immediately noticeable. The new 10-microphone array can dynamically block out more outside sound. Even without playing any media, the headphones are absurdly quiet in many different environments. It is almost ridiculously good! The biggest improvement in ANC is in handling sudden noises. Blocking out steady noise like an aeroplane engine is one thing, but blocking out cars passing by on the street, construction sites, sirens, or sudden loud noises is quite another.

Finally, two more points worth mentioning: comfort and the Sonos ecosystem. These are the most comfortable headphones I have ever worn. Even on long-haul flights of 8 to 10 hours, I wore them for nearly the entire time without any soreness, pressure, or a stuffy feeling. Lastly, I have many Sonos speakers at home, and they have added a feature that lets you transfer music from the speakers to the headphones with a single tap. It is a really cool feature, but personally I have not used it much.

My only complaint is that the carrying case needs a better zipper or mechanism, because the sticker inside keeps sticking!

Pricing and availability

The Sonos Ace Ultra went on sale today on the Sonos website and Amazon, priced at US$449, the same as the original Sonos Ace's launch price. It comes in four colours: Black, White, Agave, and Sand. I also noticed that the original Sonos Ace is currently on sale on Amazon for US$239, while stocks last. At US$240, it could also be a decent option.

Priced at US$450, the Sonos Ace Ultra firmly occupies the high-end noise-cancelling headphone market, going head-to-head with offerings from brands such as Apple, Bose, and Sony.

Final verdict

The original Sonos Ace felt like a decent first-generation product, whereas the Sonos Ace Ultra feels like a complete, mature product. As we have seen, they have not redesigned the look, but they have improved in every area that matters, and even added a few interesting new features. The sound is noticeably better, ANC is stronger and smarter, battery life is longer, the app experience is smoother, and that Agave green looks absolutely stunning.

If you already own the first-generation Sonos Ace, I think this upgrade is absolutely worth it, depending on what matters to you. If you are currently in the market for a pair of high-end headphones, I think the Sonos Ace Ultra should definitely be on your shortlist. At US$449, it is certainly not cheap, but if you want one of the very best high-end headphones out there and you are a Sonos fan, you are going to love them.
